exam: A patient with TB presents with fatigue, hyperpigmentation and orthostatic hypotension — what is the next diagnostic step and why? — Perform an 8 am serum cortisol; low level confirms adrenal insufficiency, guiding urgent steroid replacement.

A febrile child from a malaria‑endemic area has polyuria and a random glucose of 250 mg/dL — how do you differentiate stress hyperglycaemia from diabetes? — Repeat glucose after malaria treatment; persistent elevation >200 mg/dL warrants diabetes work‑up.

You see a patient with weight loss, tremor and a diffuse goitre — which bedside test helps you decide between Graves’ disease and thyroiditis? — Check for ophthalmopathy and perform a TSH; suppressed TSH points to Graves’.

In a patient on long‑term ART, you notice central obesity and hypertension — which endocrine side‑effect should you suspect and how to manage? — Lipodystrophy from protease inhibitors; address with lifestyle measures and consider switching regimen.

A woman in labour shows excessive uterine contractions after oxytocin infusion — what hormonal feedback explains this? — Positive feedback loop of oxytocin amplifies contractions; stop infusion to prevent uterine rupture.

A patient with chronic steroid use presents with hypertension and hyperglycaemia — what is the underlying hormonal mechanism? — Exogenous glucocorticoids suppress ACTH and cause insulin resistance, leading to metabolic syndrome.
ai.title: Hormonal Regulation in Clinical Medicine
ai.subject: Physiology
ai.summary: Hormones coordinate body systems; clinicians must recognise patterns of excess or deficiency, link them to common tropical diseases, and use limited investigations to guide urgent management.

b: Negative feedback: most hormones (e.g., cortisol, thyroid hormones).
Positive feedback: rare, e.g., oxytocin during labour.
sections.p: Hormones are chemical messengers released by glands into the bloodstream to regulate metabolism, growth, reproduction and stress responses. Feedback loops (negative and positive) maintain balance.

b: Hypothalamic‑pituitary‑target organ axes (e.g., HPA, HPT, HPG).
Primary vs secondary endocrine disorders.
Stress‑related cortisol rise can mask infection signs.
sections.p: Clinicians think in terms of axis dysfunction, target‑organ effects and precipitating illnesses common in low‑resource settings.

b: Hyperthyroidism → weight loss, tachycardia; consider iodine excess or Graves’ disease.
Adrenal insufficiency → hypotension, hyponatraemia; think TB adrenalitis.
Diabetes mellitus → polyuria, infection risk; malaria or steroids can precipitate hyperglycaemia.
sections.p: Endocrine disturbances present with nonspecific symptoms; linking them to local diseases (HIV, TB, malaria, schistosomiasis) helps prioritise work‑up.

t.b: Is adrenal insufficiency present? Low cortisol confirms primary/secondary insufficiency.
Distinguish primary from secondary thyroid disease. High TSH with low T4 = primary hypothyroidism.
Detect hyperglycaemia in infection or steroid use. >200 mg/dL suggests diabetes or stress hyperglycaemia.

b: Skin hyperpigmentation → chronic adrenal insufficiency.
Warm, moist skin with tremor → hyperthyroidism.
Delayed relaxation of deep tendon reflexes → hypothyroidism.
sections.p: Focus on bedside clues that point to hormonal imbalance before labs arrive.

b: Assuming low cortisol always means primary adrenal disease; TB can cause secondary suppression.
Treating hyperglycaemia without checking for infection; malaria can raise glucose.
Missing drug‑induced endocrine effects (e.g., antiretroviral‑induced lipodystrophy).
sections.p: Avoid over‑reliance on single tests and ignore local disease modifiers.

b: Hypothyroidism: start oral levothyroxine; avoid loading doses in cardiac disease.
Hyperthyroidism: beta‑blocker (propranolol) for rate control; consider thionamides if available.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, replace deficient hormones, and monitor for complications.

b: Hyperthyroidism vs sepsis – both cause tachycardia; thyroid exam and TSH help differentiate.
Cushing’s syndrome vs obesity – look for centripetal fat, striae, hypertension.
sections.p: Endocrine disorders can mimic cardiac, renal or infectious diseases.

b: TSH may be transiently suppressed in non‑thyroidal illness.
Cortisol rises with stress; a single normal level does not exclude insufficiency.
sections.p: Laboratory values may be altered by acute illness or medications.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe hypotension or shock in suspected adrenal crisis
Altered mental status with hyperglycaemic crisis
